title: How ConcurrentHashMap is made thread-safe
context: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java collections questions (2 of 2)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: Since Java 8, ConcurrentHashMap uses an array of nodes. An empty bin is filled with a compare-and-swap, which needs no lock. A non-empty bin is locked with synchronized on its first node, so writers to different bins don't interfere. Reads take no lock and rely on volatile fields. Lists in a bin turn into trees when they grow, as in HashMap. Resizing is cooperative: threads that hit a moved bin help copy it. The size is counted in a set of cells to avoid one hot counter.

points.title: CAS for empty bins
points.why: Inserting into an empty bin needs no lock, which keeps most writes cheap.

points.title: Lock per bin
points.why: Only the first node of a bin is locked, so contention stays local.

points.title: Lock-free reads
points.why: Readers use volatile reads, so they never block on writers.
